spec.summary: Speed changes are one of the most used edits in short video: a slow-motion moment, a time-lapse of a long walk, a clip played backwards, a still held on the best frame, a ramp that speeds into an action and slows down at its peak. Today every video clip plays at its own speed, forwards, and the only still is a photo. 207 lets the user set a video clip’s speed (constant), play it in reverse, freeze a frame, and ramp the speed over the clip with a curve, and see it the same in the preview and the export. The clip’s sound follows a constant speed; it is muted for ramps and reverse at first, as the work item (P2.7) says. With 206’s transitions and 205’s keyframes it completes the timeline’s picture edits for Phase 2.

US-1.text: As a creator making a Reel, I want to slow a clip down or speed it up to an exact speed, so that a jump lands in slow motion and a long walk becomes a few seconds.

US-2.text: As a vlogger, I want to play a clip backwards, so that I can rewind a moment for effect.

US-3.text: As an editor, I want to freeze the frame at the playhead for a few seconds, so that I can hold on a face or put a title over a still.

US-4.text: As a creator, I want speed ramps (presets like Montage or Hero, or my own curve), so that a clip speeds into an action and slows at its peak, like the edits in my feed.

US-5.text: As an editor, I want speed changes to keep the rest of my edit in order (later clips, transitions, keyframes, sound), and to undo them in one step.

US-6.text: As a keyboard or screen-reader user, I want to set speed, reverse, freeze and ramps without a mouse and hear what changed.

AC-1.text: A video clip has a speed from 0.1× to 10× (Q1), 1× by default, typed or chosen from presets 0.25×, 0.5×, 0.75×, 1×, 1.5×, 2×, 4×. At speed *s* the same part of the source (its in and out points) lasts (out − in) / *s* on the timeline, and the source time at *t* seconds into the clip is in + *t* × *s*. For a fixture at 0.25×, 0.5×, 2× and 10×, at 30 and 60 fps, the source time drawn at every frame of the export equals the expected list exactly (within 1 µs). Photos have no speed (their length is how long they show).

AC-2.text: Changing a clip’s speed changes its length on the timeline, not the part of the source it uses (Q2). On the main track with **Magnetic** on, later clips move with it; elsewhere a clip that would run into the next clip is refused with the reason (Q3). A change that would make the video longer than its platform’s limit (Reels 90 s web / 180 s desktop, YouTube 15 min / 3 h) is refused with the reason, as is a speed that would make the clip shorter than 0.1 s. Trimming a sped-up clip moves its in and out points by its speed (a 1 s drag at 2× uses 2 s more source). Roll, Slip, Slide and split keep each part’s speed.

AC-3.text: A video clip can play in reverse, at any constant speed: the first frame shown is its out point and the last its in point, and the source time at *t* seconds into the clip is out − *t* × *s*. Trimming its start on the timeline moves its out point and trimming its end its in point, so what the user sees at each edge is what they trim. For a fixture reversed at 1× and 2×, the source time at every frame of the export equals the expected list exactly.

AC-4.text: **Freeze frame** with a video clip under the playhead splits it there and puts a still of that exact frame between the two parts (Q4): 2 s by default, 0.1 s to 60 s, its length changed like a photo’s by dragging its end. It is drawn from the video at that source time (not a screenshot of the preview), with the clip’s box, framing and look (203, 205, its edit) carried over; it has no sound. On the main track with Magnetic on, later clips move by its length; elsewhere it is refused when it doesn’t fit, with the reason. At the clip’s first or last frame it goes before or after the clip without a split.

AC-5.text: A video clip can have a speed ramp instead of a constant speed: a curve of speed over the clip, 2 to 10 points (Q5), each a place along the clip and a speed from 0.1× to 10×, joined smoothly. Six presets set the points (Montage, Hero, Bullet, Jump cut, Flash in, Flash out, Q6), which can then be changed. The clip’s length is the time the curve takes to play through its source part, and the source time is a function of clip time that always moves forwards, starts at its in point and ends exactly at its out point (within 1 µs); a ramp never reaches the out point early or late. For a fixture with each preset and a custom curve, at 30 and 60 fps, the source time at every frame equals the expected list exactly. A ramp and reverse don’t go together on one clip in 207 (Q7).

AC-6.text: The clip’s sound follows a constant speed (Q8): over its length on the timeline it plays the same part of the source, faster or slower, at the same pitch, from 0.5× to 2×; outside that range, in reverse and with a ramp it is muted, and the inspector says why. A freeze frame is silent. Clip volume, 205’s volume keyframes and 206’s transition fades apply on the timeline as before. The export’s sound sources for a fixture with each case equal the expected list exactly.

AC-7.text: A clip’s keyframes (205) stay at the same places along the clip when its speed or ramp changes, so an animation keeps its shape over the new length (Q9). Its transitions (206) keep their lengths and are shortened to the new limit if needed, with the reason; their handles (the source beyond in and out) are taken at the clip’s speed at that edge, held at its first or last frame where the source runs out. Layers and the music are timed on the timeline and don’t move unless Magnetic moves the clips they follow today.

AC-8.text: Each change is one undo step: setting a speed (a slider drag is one step however long), reverse on or off, freeze frame, choosing a ramp preset, moving, adding or removing a ramp point (a drag is one step), and **Reset speed**. A seeded property test of 1,000 random speed, reverse, ramp, freeze, trim, split and move edits never leaves a clip whose source time leaves its in–out part, whose length differs from what its speed gives, or that overlaps another clip on its track.

AC-9.text: Speed, reverse, ramps and freeze frames are saved with the project. The document validator reads them with the other fields: speeds are clamped to 0.1×–10×, ramps with fewer than 2 or more than 10 points, unordered places or non-finite values are mended or dropped with the reason, reverse together with a ramp keeps the ramp; at least 20 malformed documents never make it throw. A project with every case round-trips document → validator → document equal; documents without speed changes stay byte-identical.

AC-10.text: The preview and the export decide which source frame to draw with one function (the same one as AC-1, AC-3, AC-5): at any time, each clip under it and the source time to show. The export draws only the frames it shows, and when the next frame it needs is past the next key frame it jumps to that key frame instead of decoding through (at 10× it never plays through the source); a freeze frame is decoded once (D3).

AC-11.text: The inspector of a selected video clip has a **Speed** group: Constant or Ramp; the speed as a field and slider with the presets (AC-1); **Reverse**; the ramp’s presets and a curve editor with its points (drag a point, double-click to add one, Delete to remove one); the clip’s new length; **Reset speed**. **Freeze frame** is in the timeline’s transport and on Shift + F with the timeline focused (Q10). On the timeline a sped-up, slowed, reversed or ramped clip shows a badge (“2×”, “0.5×”, “◀ 1×”, “Ramp”), and a freeze frame looks like a still.

AC-12.text: Everything in AC-11 works from the keyboard: the ramp’s points are focusable, ← / → move a point along the clip and ↑ / ↓ change its speed (Shift: larger steps); every control has a name and state for screen readers and each change is announced (clip, speed, new length); axe finds no serious problems in the inspector and timeline; at 360 px wide nothing scrolls sideways outside the timeline.

AC-13.text: Golden frames: a test video with a frame counter burnt in, at 0.5×, 2×, 10×, reversed, frozen and with the Hero ramp, shows at each checked frame of the export exactly the source frame AC-1, AC-3, AC-4 and AC-5 say; the paused preview shows the same frame. No regressions: projects without speed changes are pixel-identical and give identical export inputs (frames, clips, times and sound sources) to 206 for 201’s to 206’s fixtures; every existing video e2e test passes unchanged.

AC-14.text: Speed: on the reference mid-range laptop, a 1080p30 clip previews at 2× with no more dropped frames than at 1× and at 4× with at most 10 % dropped; reversed 1080p30 previews with at most 10 % dropped after its first second; a frozen frame costs no decoding while it shows. Exporting a 60-second Reel made of clips at 0.5× to 4× takes at most 25 % longer than the same Reel at 1×.

AC-15.text: `docs/MEDIA-STUDIO.md` (speed, reverse, freeze frame, ramps, their limits, the sound and the keys), `specs/lld.md` (the time mapping, the ramp curve, the sound), `CHANGELOG.md` and the in-app docs describe the change; the media studio’s “Still to do” no longer lists speed changes and reverse.

Q1.text: Speed range? _Answer (accepted 2026-10-18):_ 0.1× to 10× for constant speed and ramp points, in steps of 0.01×. Phone editors go further (CapCut 0.1×–100×), but past 10× a 1080p clip is mostly skipped frames and the export would decode most of the source to throw it away; a long time-lapse is better done by trimming. Easy to widen later.

Q2.text: What does changing the speed keep: the part of the source, or the clip’s length on the timeline? _Answer (accepted 2026-10-18):_ the part of the source (in and out points stay; the clip gets shorter or longer), as Premiere, Resolve and CapCut do by default. Keeping the length (and moving the out point) can come later as an option.

Q3.text: A slower clip on an overlay track, or on the main track with Magnetic off, that would run into the next clip? _Answer (accepted 2026-10-18):_ refused with the reason (“There is 1.2 s of room before the next clip; at 0.5× this clip needs 4 s”), like other edits that don’t fit; never silently trimmed and never overwriting the next clip.

Q4.text: What is a freeze frame? _Answer (accepted 2026-10-18):_ a still of the frame at the playhead, placed between the two halves of the split clip (what CapCut and Premiere’s Insert Frame Hold Segment do), 2 s by default, with no sound; it keeps the clip’s box, framing and look so it matches the frames around it. It is its own clip (it can be moved, trimmed, deleted, given transitions and keyframes like a photo), not a speed of 0. The alternative, holding the last frame of a clip, is the same edit with the playhead on that frame.

Q5.text: How many ramp points, and how are they joined? _Answer (accepted 2026-10-18):_ 2 to 10 points, joined by a smooth curve that doesn’t overshoot between points (so the speed never goes outside the points’ range or below 0.1×). Points are places along the clip’s source part (0 to 100 %), so trimming keeps the curve’s shape over what’s left.

Q6.text: Which ramp presets? _Answer (accepted 2026-10-18):_ six, after CapCut’s familiar set, with our own numbers: **Montage** (fast–slow–fast–slow–fast), **Hero** (normal, slow in the middle, normal), **Bullet** (fast, very slow in the middle, fast), **Jump cut** (normal, a short fast burst, normal), **Flash in** (fast into normal), **Flash out** (normal into fast). Each is just a starting set of points.

Q7.text: Ramps with reverse? _Answer (accepted 2026-10-18):_ not in 207: turning on Reverse sets the clip back to a constant speed (and says so), and choosing a ramp turns Reverse off. Reverse with a ramp is rare and doubles the cases to get right; it can come later.

Q8.text: The sound at a constant speed: same pitch, or pitch follows the speed (“chipmunk”)? _Answer (accepted 2026-10-18):_ same pitch from 0.5× to 2×, muted outside it, in reverse and with ramps (the work item says muted for ramps and reverse at first). The preview gets the same pitch from the browser (audio elements keep pitch by default); the export needs a time-stretch of its own (no new library), which is the main cost of this feature. The cheaper choice is pitch following the speed (a simple resample, same in preview and export); it sounds like a tape played fast or slow. The maintainer chose same pitch on 2026-10-18.

Q9.text: Keyframes when the speed changes: stay at the same timeline times, or the same places along the clip? _Answer (accepted 2026-10-18):_ the same places along the clip (scaled with its length), so a zoom that ran over the whole clip still does; keyframes are timed from the clip’s start on the timeline (205) and stay so.

Q10.text: Keys? _Answer (accepted 2026-10-18):_ Shift + F for Freeze frame with the timeline focused (F alone is free today but reads as “fit” in other editors). No key for speed: it is in the inspector. Ctrl + R (Premiere’s speed dialog) is the browser’s reload and is left alone.

Q11.text: Agent tools (MCP) for speed? _Answer (accepted 2026-10-18):_ not in 207; they come with the other timeline tools in 212, like 206’s transitions.

sections.title: Non-Functional Requirements
sections.markdown:
- **Performance:** at 1× and without a ramp nothing changes: projects without speed changes preview and export within 5 % of 206 (AC-13); a speed change costs only the decoding it needs (fast clips skip frames in the export, freezes decode once); preview at high speeds and in reverse may drop frames within AC-14’s limits.
- **Accuracy:** the source frame shown at every exported frame is exactly the one the speed, reverse, ramp or freeze says (AC-1, AC-3–AC-5, AC-10, AC-13); a clip’s length never drifts from its speed (AC-8).
- **Accessibility:** every action works from the keyboard and is announced; names and states for screen readers; the curve editor has a non-pointer way to set every point (AC-12).
- **Compatibility:** web and desktop alike; no new dependency; every existing project opens and exports unchanged (AC-9, AC-13).
- **Free and open source:** every speed feature is for everyone, on the web and in the desktop app.

sections.title: Out of Scope
sections.markdown:
- Speeds outside 0.1×–10×; keeping the clip’s length when the speed changes (Q1, Q2).
- Sound for ramps and reverse, and pitch-kept sound outside 0.5×–2× (Q8): later, with the audio work.
- Ramps together with reverse (Q7); frame blending or optical-flow slow motion (frames are repeated when slowed).
- Speed for photos, layers or the music; speed keyframed through 205’s keyframes (ramps are their own curve).
- Agent tools for speed (212, Q11).

risks.text: **Reverse playback cost** (§3, AC-14): decoders only go forwards, so reverse means decoding a key-frame group to show its frames backwards. Mitigation: a spike task first with the fake decoder (chunked backward lanes within the byte budget); preview reverse at stage size (D4); if a long-GOP phone video still drops too many frames in 290, the preview holds frames (as it does today when behind) while the export stays exact.

**Same-pitch export sound** (§5, AC-6): our own WSOLA can warble on music or clip at window edges. Mitigation: unit tests on sines and on window joins (no step larger than the signal's own between samples); the 50 ms carry-over between windows; a listening check in 290 with speech and music at 0.5×, 0.75×, 1.5×, 2×; if it isn't good enough, fall back to pitch following the speed (Q8's cheaper choice) after asking the maintainer.

**Missing one `clip.in + local`** (§3): a place left on the old mapping shows the wrong frame only at a speed ≠ 1. Mitigation: every site goes through `sourceAt` in one task, with a grep check that none is left; the golden frames in 290 cover preview and export.

**Ramp numerics** (§1, AC-5): an inverse that drifts reaches `out` early or late. Mitigation: the table's end is pinned to the exact integral and the last frame to `out`; tests against a 100× finer reference for every preset at 30 and 60 fps.

**Clip length floor** (§2): `clipLength` keeps a 0.1 s floor that would break the mapping for a tiny clip at 10×. Mitigation: speeds that would go under it are refused, so the floor never applies to a sped-up clip.

sections.title: Approach
sections.markdown:
Speed is data on a video clip, and **one function** turns a clip's time into a source time: `sourceAt(clip, local)` in a new `engine/speed.ts`. Today `clip.in + local` is written out in nine places (the export's frames and trace, the preview's frames, the stage's peek and fallback video, the preview sound, the sound plan, the pool's prime, the lanes' handles); each becomes a call to `sourceAt`, and `clipLength` learns the speed, so every rule that already asks `clipLength` / `frameStack` / `audioPlan` (packing, Magnetic, gaps, the export's frames, transitions' room, the videos-at-once limit) follows without change (Constitution VIII, AC-10). Under D-033 every task is proven by unit tests; e2e, golden frames, timing and listening checks go to 290.

**§1 The time mapping (new `engine/speed.ts`, AC-1, AC-3, AC-5, AC-10).** A video clip gets `speed?` (0.1–10, missing = 1, Q1), `reverse?: true`, `ramp?: RampPoint[]` (2–10 points `{ at, v }`: `at` a share 0–1 of the source part `in`–`out`, `v` a speed; a ramp replaces `speed`, and never goes with `reverse`, Q7) and `freeze?: number` (§4). Pure functions: `clipLength` (timeline.ts) becomes `(out − in) / speed` for a constant speed and the ramp's play time for a ramp; `sourceAt(clip, local)` = `in + local × s`, `out − local × s` reversed, the ramp's inverse for a ramp, the frozen time for a freeze; `localAt(clip, source)` its inverse (for trims, split and the timeline's thumbnails). Outside 0…length (transition handles, 206) it goes on at the speed of that edge and the caller clamps to the file as today. A ramp's speed over the source part is a monotone cubic through its points (curve.ts's Fritsch–Carlson spline, no overshoot, Q5); its play time T(p) = (out − in) × ∫₀ᵖ du / v(u) is tabulated once per ramp (512 steps, adaptive Simpson within each step split at the points: plain Simpson misses 1 µs on steep curves; cached on the ramp array by a WeakMap) and inverted by Newton steps on the table, so `sourceAt(clip, length)` lands on `out` within 1 µs (AC-5). Presets (Q6) are data: `RAMP_PRESETS` = Montage, Hero, Bullet, Jump cut, Flash in, Flash out.

**§2 Edits (`engine/edits.ts`, new `engine/speedEdits.ts`, AC-2, AC-7).** `setSpeed(clips, id, speed | ramp | reverse, ctx)` builds the new clip, keeps in and out (Q2), and then reuses the existing rules: on the main track with Magnetic on, `pack` moves the later clips; elsewhere `checkTrack` refuses an overlap with Q3's reason ("There is 1.2 s of room before the next clip; at 0.5× this clip needs 4 s"); the platform's length limit (`TOO_LONG`) and a new shortest length (a speed that would make the clip shorter than 0.1 s is refused, as `clipLength`'s floor would otherwise break the mapping) refuse the rest. `trim` turns the drag (timeline seconds) into source seconds with `localAt` / `sourceAt`, so a 1 s drag at 2× uses 2 s of source and a reversed clip's start edge moves its out point (AC-3); a ramped clip's edge moves along its curve, which stays over a fixed source span (`rampSpan`, D2, amended 2026-10-18). `split` gives both parts the speed and reverse, and each the same ramp and span (D2). Roll, Slip and Slide go through `trim` / in-out moves and keep each part's speed. Keyframes (Q9): `scaleKeys(keys, newLength / oldLength)` in keyframes.ts after a speed or ramp change. Transitions (206): `tidyTransitions` already clamps them to the new room; their handles come from §1's edge speed.

**§3 Rendering and decoding (`stack.ts`, `video.ts`, `decodePool.ts`, `frameSource.ts`, `videoExport.ts`, `previewFrame.ts`, `VideoStage.tsx`, AC-10).** `StackItem` gains nothing: drawers call `sourceAt(item.clip, item.local)`. The export job (`videoExportJob.ts` copies clip fields by name) carries `speed`, `reverse`, `ramp`, `freeze`. The pool: (a) a lane's window (`PoolClip`) is the source span the clip shows, from `sourceAt` at its first and last shown local times (with handles), so a reversed clip's lane covers out → in; (b) **skipping**: a reader keeps reading forward only while the wanted frame is within the current group of pictures; past the next key frame it restarts there (`FrameSource.keyAfter(time)` from Mediabunny's key packets), so a 10× export decodes from key frames rather than through the whole source (D3); (c) **reverse**: a reversed lane decodes backwards in chunks (from the key frame before the wanted time up to it), holds that chunk's frames within the pool's byte budget and hands them out newest first; the preview's reversed lanes decode at stage size (`maxWidth`) so a chunk fits (D4). A spike task proves (c) with the fake frame source first (risk 1). A freeze frame's lane decodes its one frame once and holds it.

**§4 Freeze frame (`speedEdits.ts`, `videoClips.ts`, AC-4).** A freeze frame is a video clip with `freeze` = the source time it shows and `dur` its length (2 s default, 0.1–60 s), the same file, box, framing, look and keyframes held at their values at the cut (one key each, as split gives its parts, so nothing jumps; D-051) as the clip it came from; `clipLength` uses `dur` like a photo's and it has no sound (D1). `freezeFrame(clips, id, local, ctx)` splits the clip at the playhead (none at its first or last frame) and inserts the freeze between the parts: on the main track with Magnetic on the later clips move by its length; elsewhere it is refused when it doesn't fit, with the reason. Its end is dragged like a photo's (`trim` treats it as a photo).

**§5 Sound (`soundPlan.ts`, new `engine/timeStretch.ts`, `videoExport.ts`, `previewSound.ts`, AC-6).** `SoundSource` gains `rate` (source seconds per timeline second, missing = 1). `clipSounds` leaves out a clip whose speed is outside 0.5–2, reversed, ramped or frozen (`soundMuted(clip)` gives the reason the inspector shows); the rest get `rate = speed`. The preview sets `playbackRate = speed × nudge` on the clip's element with `preservesPitch` on (the browser keeps the pitch). The export decodes `[from, from + length × rate]` and runs it through `timeStretch(samples, rate, sampleRate)`: WSOLA (waveform-similarity overlap-add, 40 ms Hann frames, 50 % overlap, ±10 ms search; our own ~150 lines, no new dependency) to the timeline length, then schedules it as one buffer per window; windows carry 50 ms of the previous one's input so cuts between 10-second windows don't click (D5). Volume, 205's volume keyframes and 206's edges stay on the gain node in timeline time, unchanged.

**§6 Store actions (new `state/videoSpeed.ts`, `state/videoClips.ts`, AC-8).** `setClipSpeed`, `setClipReverse`, `setClipRamp` (preset or points), `moveRampPoint`, `addRampPoint`, `removeRampPoint`, `resetSpeed`, `freezeFrame`: each one `change()` with a coalescing key (`speed:<id>`, `ramp:<id>:<point>`), so a slider or point drag is one undo step; refusals are toasts and announcements, as 202's edits. Turning on reverse with a ramp drops the ramp (and says so); choosing a ramp turns reverse off (Q7). A seeded property test runs 1,000 random speed, reverse, ramp, freeze, trim, split and move edits and checks the invariants after each (AC-8).

**§7 Saving (`projectGate.ts`, `projectDoc.ts`, AC-9).** `readClip` reads the four fields through `mergeSpeed(raw, dropped)`: speeds clamped to 0.1–10, ramps with fewer than 2 or more than 10 points, unordered or non-finite places dropped or mended with the reason, a ramp with reverse keeps the ramp, `freeze` clamped into the file. A clip at 1× forward without ramp or freeze writes none of the fields, so documents without speed changes stay byte-identical.

**§8 Inspector and timeline (new `components/studio/SpeedGroup.tsx`, `RampEditor.tsx`; `ClipInspector.tsx`, `PictureRow.tsx`, `timelineRows.ts`, `Transport.tsx`, `Timeline.tsx`, AC-11, AC-12).** The Speed group: Constant / Ramp; the speed as a field and slider (log scale, 0.1–10) with the presets; Reverse; the new length; Reset speed; for a ramp the six presets and `RampEditor`, an SVG curve with focusable points (drag, double-click to add, Delete to remove; ← / → along the clip, ↑ / ↓ speed, Shift for larger steps), each change announced. The badge on a clip ("2×", "0.5×", "◀ 1×", "Ramp", a still for a freeze) is a pure `speedBadge(clip)` in `timelineRows.ts`; thumbnails and the description use `sourceAt`. Freeze frame is a Transport button and Shift + F with the timeline focused (Q10). Unit tests cover the pure helpers; the UI itself is checked in 290.

sections.title: Data Structures & Interfaces
Techniques
sections.markdown:
- **One mapping, everywhere.** `sourceAt` replaces every `clip.in + local`; a grep for that pattern in `src/` is empty when §3 is done (checked in the task). At 1× forward without a ramp it returns exactly `in + local` (same floating-point operations), so 206's export inputs are bit-identical (AC-13).
- **Ramps as a monotone spline over the source.** curve.ts's Fritsch–Carlson spline joins the points without overshoot (Q5), so v stays within the points' range and above 0.1×; the play-time table is computed once per ramp and cached, and the inverse is Newton on the table, with the end pinned to `out` exactly.
- **Reuse the edit rules.** Speed edits build the new clip and hand it to `checkTrack` / `pack` / `limitVideos` / `tidyTransitions` as 202's edits do, so Magnetic, refusals, the videos-at-once limit and transitions follow without new code paths.
- **WSOLA** for same-pitch sound in the export: overlap-add of Hann-windowed frames taken from the source at the rate, each shifted within ±10 ms to the best cross-correlation with the previous output; pure Float32Array in and out, unit-tested on sines (pitch kept: zero crossings per second within 1 %) and on length (within one frame).
- **Reverse decoding in chunks** keeps the pool's limits: a chunk is at most the pool's `ahead` × 4 frames or the byte budget, whichever is smaller.
- **Announcements** through the timeline's live region, as 202–206 do ("Clip 2: 0.5×, now 8.4 s").

sections.title: Decisions for the maintainer (accepted 2026-10-18: D1–D5 as recommended)
sections.markdown:
- **D1 — What a freeze frame is in the data.** _Recommended:_ a video clip with `freeze` (the source time it shows) and `dur` (its length): it keeps the file, box, framing, look and keyframes with no new clip kind, and every rule that handles video clips (tracks, transitions, the videos-at-once limit, saving) takes it as it is. _Alternative:_ a third clip kind `still` (clearer in the data, but every `kind === 'photo' | 'video'` switch, the gate and the export job would need a new case).
- **D2 — Ramps when a clip is trimmed or split.** _Recommended:_ the curve is **cut**: points stay at the same source moments, the speed at the new edge becomes a point there, points outside are dropped (and a trim outwards extends the edge speed), so what plays at every moment that is kept doesn't change and the trimmed edge shows what was there. Q5's "trimming keeps the curve's shape over what's left" read this way. **Amended 2026-10-18 (T043, D-050):** cutting re-fits the spline through fewer points, which changed what plays between them (a split Bullet ramp up to 0.59 s, 32 %); instead the ramp keeps its curve over a fixed source span (`rampSpan`, set on the first trim or split; missing = in–out) and trims and splits only move in and out along it, so every kept frame plays exactly as before and trimming back out restores the clip. _Alternative:_ the curve is **stretched** over what's left (its shares kept), which changes the speed of frames the user didn't touch.
- **D3 — AC-10's "decodes only the frames it draws".** Compressed video can only be decoded from a key frame, so at 10× the export can't decode just the frames it draws. _Recommended:_ reword AC-10 to "the export draws only the frames it shows, and when the next frame it needs is past the next key frame it jumps there instead of decoding through (at 10× it never plays through the source)", and measure it with the fake decoder (frames decoded per frame drawn). _Alternative:_ keep the wording and accept it can't be met literally.
- **D4 — Reverse in the preview.** _Recommended:_ reversed lanes in the preview decode at the stage's size, in backward chunks within the pool's byte budget (the export decodes at its own size as today); the first second may drop frames (AC-14). _Alternative:_ reverse decoded at full size (fewer frames per chunk, more key-frame restarts, more dropped frames).
- **D5 — Sound in the preview vs the export.** _Recommended:_ the preview uses the browser's own pitch keeping (`preservesPitch`), the export our WSOLA: both keep the pitch, but they won't be sample-identical (the picture is). _Alternative:_ run our WSOLA in the preview too (an AudioWorklet and decoding the clip's sound up front: much more code and memory for a small gain).
- **Spec changes with the plan:** AC-10's wording (D3) and the shortest length (a speed that would make a clip shorter than 0.1 s is refused) go into the spec's Changelog when the plan is approved.

tasks.intro:
**Plan:** `./plan.md`
Legend: `[P]` = can run in parallel with the previous task; 👤 = needs a person. Each task lists files and the proving test.
Test-first: each "failing" task must fail before its paired implementation makes it pass. Tasks run one at a time in the main session.
Tasks are proven by unit tests only (D-033); the e2e, golden-frame, listening and timing checks are listed in `290` ("Deferred checks collected from the phase": 207 AC-6, AC-11, AC-12, AC-13, AC-14).
When a task is done, record a **Result (YYYY-MM-DD):** note with `npm run specs -- done 207 Txxx --result "…"`.
